title: Two branches checked out at once, one repository
summary: Stop stashing every time an urgent fix arrives. A worktree gives you a second working directory on the same repository, with its own branch, sharing all the objects.
mental_model: A repository has one object database and can have many working directories. Each worktree checks out a different branch and has its own index and HEAD, but commits land in the same shared store instantly.

write.content:
WORK_IN_PROGRESS = True
HALF_DONE = 'do not commit yet'

steps.title: The situation stash usually solves badly
steps.why: You are mid-refactor with uncommitted work, and a production fix is needed on main. Stashing works but costs you the running test process, the open editor state, and your place.

steps.title: Add a second working directory
steps.why: `worktree add` creates a real directory with main checked out. Your current directory is untouched — the half-finished refactor stays exactly as it is, uncommitted.
steps.expect: A new worktree listed, and your own status still showing the modified file.

verify.label: your uncommitted work was never touched

steps.title: Work in the other directory
steps.why: It is a normal working tree: edit, add, commit. The commit goes into the shared object database immediately, so the main repository can see it without any pushing or fetching.

verify.label: the commit landed on main from the other worktree

steps.title: See it from the original directory
steps.why: No fetch, no pull. `git log main` from here already shows the commit, because there is only one object store and one set of refs.
steps.expect: The hotfix commit visible, and your refactor still uncommitted and untouched.

steps.title: Try to check out the same branch twice
steps.why: Git refuses: two worktrees on one branch would let two indexes fight over the same ref. The restriction is the reason worktrees are safe rather than confusing.
steps.expect: fatal: 'main' is already used by worktree at ... — exit code 128.

steps.title: Look at the plumbing
steps.why: The linked worktree has a `.git` *file* pointing back at the main repository's `.git/worktrees/<name>` directory, which holds its own HEAD and index. Small, cheap, and disposable.
steps.expect: A gitdir: pointer, and per-worktree HEAD and index files.

steps.title: Clean up when the fix ships
steps.why: `worktree remove` deletes the directory and its metadata. If the directory was deleted by hand instead, `worktree prune` clears the leftover bookkeeping.
steps.expect: One worktree again — and the hotfix commit still safely on main.

verify.label: …while its commit remains, because objects are shared
the hotfix was committed to main from a second worktree
your uncommitted refactor survived the whole exercise, unstashed
the temporary worktree was cleaned up

pitfalls: A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time. This is a feature — it prevents two indexes disagreeing about the same ref.
Deleting a worktree directory by hand leaves stale metadata. Run `git worktree prune`, or use `git worktree remove`.
Worktrees share hooks, config and objects but NOT the index or stash. `git stash` in one is invisible in the other.
`git worktree add -b <new> <path>` creates the branch as it goes, which is usually what you want for a hotfix.
cheatsheet: second working directory on an existing branch

every working directory and its branch
clear metadata for directories deleted by hand
